title: News feed
summary: The Twitter problem: a ranked feed of posts from everyone you follow, assembled in under 300 ms, when some of the people you follow have 50 million followers.
interviewerPrompt: Let's design a news feed, like the home timeline on Twitter. Users follow other users and see their posts. How would you build it?

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many users, and how active are they?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 500M registered users, 300M daily active. A daily user opens the feed about 10 times a day.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How much do people post?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About one post per daily user per day on average, so roughly 300M posts a day. Posts are short text, optionally with images.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many accounts does a user follow, and how many followers do accounts have?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The median user follows 200 accounts. Most accounts have a few hundred followers, but a few accounts have 50M.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the feed chronological or ranked?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Ranked: the most relevant recent posts first. You do not need to design the machine-learning model, but the feed must be ranked within the latency budget.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How fast must the feed load?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The first page must be returned in under 300 ms at p99, measured at our servers.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How fresh must it be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A new post should appear in followers' feeds within a minute. Authors must see their own post immediately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the feed include posts from accounts the user does not follow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not for this interview. Only followed accounts; recommendations are out of scope.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How far back can a user scroll?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Most sessions read the first page or two. Users can keep scrolling into older posts, and that may be slower.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about deleted posts, blocks and mutes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A deleted post must disappear from feeds quickly, and a user must never see posts from accounts they blocked or muted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How spiky is traffic?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Assume the busiest hour runs at about 3 times the daily average, and live events can push posting much higher for a few minutes.

deepDiveQuestions: Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or a hybrid: what do you do about accounts with 50M followers?
What exactly is in the feed cache, how big is it, and what happens to users whose feed is not cached?
How do you rank the feed inside the latency budget, and what happens when ranking is slow?
How does pagination work with cursors when new posts keep arriving and the order is ranked?

runChallenge.title: Evening peak with a zone down
runChallenge.description: Run at the 3× evening peak (about 156k feed pages and 10k posts a second) and lose the busiest availability zone after 10 s. Feed pages and post creates must stay under 300 ms at p99 with under 0.1% errors and no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: Choosing pure fan-out on write and not noticing that one post from a 50M-follower account means 50M cache writes, minutes of lag and a backlog for everyone else.
Choosing pure fan-out on read, which turns every feed load into 200 queries and a merge, and cannot meet 300 ms at 156k feed loads a second.
Storing full post bodies in every follower's feed, multiplying storage by the follower count and making edits and deletes impossible to apply.
Paginating with page numbers or offsets, so new posts arriving at the top push items down and the user sees duplicates or skips posts.
Fanning out to every follower, including the many who have not opened the app in months.
Putting the ranking model on the critical path with no timeout or fallback, so a slow ranker makes the whole feed fail.
Forgetting the author: with asynchronous fan-out, the author refreshes and does not see their own post.
Sizing the timeline cache by reads, when fan-out writes are about nine times the peak read rate.
